prompt: What are the best practices for application secrets management?
completion:
## Application Secrets Management – A Practical “Cheat Sheet” | **Stage** | **What to do** | **Why it matters** | **Typical Tools / Examples** | |-----------|----------------|---------------------|-----------------------------| | **Planning** | • Identify every secret (DB passwords, API keys, certificates, OAuth tokens, etc.)
• Classify by sensitivity (high, medium, low)
• Define retention & rotation windows | Gives you a clear inventory and risk profile | Spreadsheet/issue tracker, GitHub Issues, Jira, or a dedicated “Secrets Inventory” repo | | **Storage** | • Never hard‑code or commit secrets to VCS
• Store secrets in a dedicated, encrypted secrets store
• Use one store per environment (dev, staging, prod) | Prevents accidental leaks & makes rotation easier | HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager, Kubernetes Secrets (with encryption‑at‑rest) | | **Access Control** | • Apply least‑privilege IAM roles or RBAC for secrets
• Use MFA for human access
• Rotate service‑account keys regularly | Limits blast radius & auditability | IAM policies, Vault policies, Azure RBAC, GCP IAM | | **Injection** | • Inject secrets into the runtime environment (env vars, mounted files, API calls)
• Keep secrets in memory only – never write to disk
• Never expose secrets in logs | Keeps secrets out of the filesystem & reduces attack surface | Docker secrets, Kubernetes secrets (mounted as files), Vault Agent / Consul Template, Spring Cloud Vault | | **Encryption** | • Encrypt secrets at rest in the vault
• Use TLS/SSL for secrets transport
• Encrypt the secrets file if you must ship them to a container | Guarantees confidentiality even if the vault is compromised | Vault's AES‑256‑GCM, AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault keys, GCP KMS | | **Rotation** | • Define rotation policies (daily, weekly, on‑call, after breach)
• Automate rotation with the secrets manager
• Update dependent services automatically (webhooks, polling) | Keeps secrets fresh and reduces the damage window | Vault dynamic secrets, AWS Secrets Manager rotation Lambda, Azure Key Vault auto‑rotate | | **Audit & Monitoring** | • Log every read/write/rotation
• Alert on unusual patterns (multiple reads, changes in dev vs prod)
• Periodically review access logs | Detect misuse early & prove compliance | CloudWatch / Azure Monitor, Splunk, Datadog, native Vault audit logs | | **Development / CI‑CD** | • Use secret‑management plugins in your CI pipeline (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables, Jenkins credentials)
• Never expose secrets in build logs
• Scan code for accidental leaks | Keeps secrets out of the codebase & CI logs | GitHub Secrets, GitLab CI variables, Vault‑CLI in GitHub Actions, GitGuardian | | **Leak Prevention** | • Run secret‑scanning tools on pull‑requests (TruffleHog, Gitleaks, GitLeaks)
• Enforce pre‑commit hooks
• Conduct regular “security reviews” of PRs | Catch accidental commits before they hit prod | pre-commit hooks, CodeQL, SonarQube | | **Disaster Recovery** | • Back up the vault (including key material) to an off‑site location
• Test vault restore regularly | Guarantees you can recover if the vault fails | Vault replication, AWS Backup for Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault recoverable | | **Segmentation** | • Keep secrets per micro‑service or per environment
• Don’t share a database password between unrelated services | Limits the impact if a single secret leaks | Kubernetes namespaces, Vault namespaces, AWS Secrets Manager prefixes | --- ### The “Secret‑as‑Code” Workflow (Illustration) 1. **Define** ```yaml # secrets.yaml dev: db_password: prod: db_password: ``` Store this in a *secure repo* with limited read access. 2. **Provision** ```bash vault kv put secret/dev/db_password value="dev-secret" vault kv put secret/prod/db_password value="prod-secret" ``` 3. **Consume** ```yaml # Docker Compose example environment: DB_PASSWORD: "{{ lookup('vaultkv', 'secret/prod/db_password') }}" ``` The compose file never contains the raw password. 4. **Rotate** ```bash vault kv put secret/prod/db_password value="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" ``` Or let Vault generate a new dynamic credential. 5. **Audit** ```bash vault audit enable file file_path=/var/log/vault_audit.log ``` --- ## Quick‑Start Checklist | ✅ | Item | Note | |----|------|------| | 1 | No secrets in source control | Use `.gitignore` or dedicated secret repo | | 2 | Secrets stored in a vault | E.g., Vault, AWS, Azure, GCP | | 3 | Secrets encrypted in transit | TLS/SSL mandatory | | 4 | Least‑privilege IAM/RBAC | Use fine‑grained policies | | 5 | Secrets never in logs | Filter logs for secret patterns | | 6 | Automated rotation | Daily/weekly or after key compromise | | 7 | Audit & alerting | Log every access, set alerts | | 8 | Secret scanning in CI | Pre‑commit hooks + PR checks | | 9 | Secure backup & DR | Replicate vault, test restore | |10 | MFA for human access | Adds second factor for secret ops | --- ## Common Pitfalls to Avoid | ❌ | Mistake | Remedy | |----|---------|--------| | Hard‑coding credentials | Remove and store in vault | | Storing secrets in environment files (`.env`) on disk | Use vault or Docker/K8s secrets | | Using the same secret for multiple services | Give each service its own secret | | Rotating secrets manually without automation | Configure auto‑rotation | | Not encrypting secrets at rest | Enable KMS/HSM encryption | | Logging secrets | Sanitize logs or drop them entirely | --- ### Bottom Line Treat application secrets like any other sensitive asset: * **Keep them out of the codebase** * **Store them in a trusted vault** * **Control who and what can read them** * **Rotate them regularly** * **Audit every access** * **Integrate secret management into the CI/CD pipeline** With this disciplined approach, you’ll dramatically reduce the risk of accidental exposure, meet compliance requirements, and keep your production systems secure.
